study.title: Leviticus 5 - Cultivated Culp and Affordable Atonement
study.overview: Leviticus 5 continues the instructions on the sin offering and expands the theme to concrete cases: omission of testimony, contact with impurity, thoughtless oaths, flaws linked to holy things and unintentional infringements. The chapter shows that sin is not treated only as an external act, but as a real guilt before the LORD, even when one only realizes later. At the same time, God provides for means of atonement proportional to the condition of each one, from an animal of the flock to flour, so that no one will be without access to forgiveness because of poverty.

outline.title: Blame for omission, impurity and oath, with confession and sacrifice
outline.explanation: The first verses present situations in which the person becomes guilty: hiding what he knows when he is called to witness, touch something unclean, or speak a precipitated oath. The decisive point is that, in perceiving guilt, he must confess it and bring an offering for sin so that the priest will make atonement and there be forgiveness.

outline.title: Provision for the poor: from animal to flour
outline.explanation: If the person cannot bring a lamb, the law provides for two rolls or two pigeons; if not possible, flour is admitted without olive oil or incense. The gradation of the offerings shows that the atonement is required of all, but also that the Lord does not close the way of forgiveness to the poor.

outline.title: Failure in holy things and sins for ignorance
outline.explanation: The second half deals with offenses against the sanctified things to the LORD and from transgressions committed without purpose. In such cases, the sinner must bring a ram, repair the injury with an increase of one fifth and yet recognize that it was infraction against the LORD, even without deliberate intention.

study.context: This chapter is part of Leviticus's sacrificiles instructions and takes up the matter of the sin offering and the guilt offering. The notes provided highlight that the cases listed here are concrete examples of sins covered by this system of atonement and that the legislation considers both faults related to worship and damage to consecrated things. The text also shows concern in adjusting the offer to the supplier's economic condition.
study.theology: Chapter theology emphasizes that guilt before God can arise from actions, omissions, ignorance or recklessness, and not just by conscious rebellion. Sin is treated as something real even when one only later recognizes his responsibility. Therefore, confession is indispensable: the rite without admission of guilt would be empty. Another central point is the mercy ordained by God, which establishes means of atonement proportional to the capacity of the offering, without relativizing divine holiness. The holiness of the LORD demands reparation; the grace of the LORD provides a way for this reparation. In the case of holy things, the requirement of restitution with addition shows that guilt is not only spiritual, but also involves objective damage that needs to be corrected. By saying that the person "certainly has transgressed against the Lord," the chapter states that every moral and cultural offense, even when it seems small or involuntary, has weight before God.

scholarViews.insight: The omission of testimony is not neutral; it actively helps the guilty and, when recognized, requires confession and offer to remove guilt.
The chapter also provides for offers for the poor, showing that poverty does not prevent access to atonement and forgiveness.
Even when the offense was made without intention, the person must still bring sacrifice, for guilt remains real before God.

questions: In which areas can I be omitting something that I know to be true or necessary, even without lying directly?
How does confession change the way I view my sin, rather than treating forgiveness as something automatic?
How can I apply the principle of this chapter to repair damage that I caused, and not just ask for forgiveness in words?
study.practice: Practice honesty before God and people: recognize clearly any sin you have ever realized, without minimizing or justifying. If there is concrete damage, try to repair it as possible, remembering that the chapter includes restitution in addition to confession. Also remember that God's grace does not exclude the poor nor the weak; therefore, does not use personal limitations as an excuse to remain without treating sin.
study.uncertainty: The given text does not bring an inspired division of verses into paragraphs, so the above structure is an interpretive organization for study purposes. The scores of the commentators in English were summarized in Portuguese; where there were multiple details, only the most directly present point in each note was chosen. There is no basis for the notes provided to state with certainty additional historical details beyond the sacrificial system described in the chapter.
